'''Zuleyma Tang-Martínez''' (born in Venezuela, March 9, 1945) is a Venezuelan emeritus professor of biology at the [[University of Missouri–St. Louis]].  Earlier in her career (up until the early 1990s) she published under her former married name, Zuleyma Tang Halpin.

== Early life and education ==
Tang-Martínez was born in [[Venezuela]] on March 9, 1945.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=http://news.stlpublicradio.org/post/zuleyma-tang-martinez-devotes-life-studying-animal-behavior#stream/0|title=Zuleyma Tang-Martinez devotes life to studying animal behavior|last=Ross|first=Gloria S.|access-date=November 12, 2018|language=en}}</ref> She and her family lived in ethnically segregated camps that were operated by an American oil company.<ref name=":0" />  Her father was a company accountant, permitting Tang-Martínez to be among the very few Venezuelans to be raised and attend school in the American camps.<ref name=":0" /> In 1960, she was sent by her parents to attend a Catholic, all-girls, boarding high school in Tampa FL because the oil camp schools did not go beyond the 8th grade. She completed high school in 1963; the nuns at the high school convinced her to go to college as a pre-med student, despite the fact that her parents had planned only on her finishing high school – as she was the first in her family to complete a high school education. She received her bachelor's degree cum laude from Saint Louis University, graduating in 1967 with a degree in biology.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.umsl.edu/~biology/About%20the%20Department/Faculty/tang.html|title=Zuleyma Tang-Martinez|website=www.umsl.edu|language=en|access-date=November 12, 2018|archive-date=October 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191010021226/http://www.umsl.edu/~biology/About%20the%20Department/Faculty/tang.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> She moved to the [[University of California, Berkeley]] for her graduate studies, earning a master's degree in 1970 (specializing in cancer research) and a PhD in 1974 in Zoology (specializing in animal behavior).<ref name=":1" /> Tang-Martínez was a [[postdoctoral researcher]] at the [[University of British Columbia]].<ref name=":1" /> For her dissertation she developed the habituation-discrimination technique in order to study individual discrimination by odors in the Mongolian gerbil ''[[Meriones unguiculatus]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Halpin|first=Z. T.|date=June 1974|title=Individual differences in the biological odors of the Mongolian gerbil, (Meriones unguiculatus)|journal=Behavioral Biology|volume=11|issue=2|pages=253–259|issn=0091-6773|pmid=4847527|doi=10.1016/s0091-6773(74)90449-0}}</ref>

== Career ==
Tang-Martínez was appointed [[assistant professor]] at the [[University of Missouri–St. Louis]] in 1976, the institution where she spent the rest of her career.  She was very active in professional societies, especially with the American Society of Zoologists (now the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology) where she was elected as chair of the Division of Animal Behavior. In the Animal Behavior Society, her primary scientific organization, she served as chair of the Animal Care Committee, the Latin American Affairs Committee, and the Diversity Committee. In 1991 she was elected to the 4-year presidential sequence, serving as ABS president from 1993 to 1994.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=http://www.animalbehaviorsociety.org/web/about-history.php|title=Animal Behavior Society|access-date=November 12, 2018|language=en}}</ref>

She studied social behavior, communication, and kin recognition of animals, as well as various aspects of dispersal, particularly with regards to how social structure impacts the genetics of populations.  In 1987 she co-edited ''Mammalian Dispersal Patterns: The Effects of Social Structure on Population Genetics'' with [[Diane Chepko-Sade]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/M/bo5967272.html|title=Mammalian Dispersal Patterns |publisher=University of Chicago Press }}</ref> More recently, she has challenged the theory of [[Angus John Bateman]] and [[Robert Trivers]] that male fruit flies behave more promiscuously due to their ability to produce millions of small sperm, and that this explains universal differences between male and female sexual behavior.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tang-Martínez|first=Zuleyma|date=May 2016|title=Rethinking Bateman's Principles: Challenging Persistent Myths of Sexually Reluctant Females and Promiscuous Males|journal=Journal of Sex Research|volume=53|issue=4–5|pages=532–559|doi=10.1080/00224499.2016.1150938|issn=1559-8519|pmid=27074147|s2cid=34715649}}</ref> She has argued against the universal application of [[Bateman's principle]] particularly with regards to the stereotypes of male and female sexual behaviour in humans.<ref>{{cite news |last=Tang-Martinez |first=Zuleyma |title=Data should smash the biological myth of promiscuous males and sexually coy females |website=The Conversation |date=January 20, 2017 |url=https://theconversation.com/data-should-smash-the-biological-myth-of-promiscuous-males-and-sexually-coy-females-59665 |access-date=July 27, 2025 |language=en}}</ref> Her research was discussed in [[Angela Saini]]'s [[Inferior: How Science Got Women Wrong and the New Research That's Rewriting the Story]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=U5DEDgAAQBAJ&dq=zuleyma+tang-martinez&pg=PA127|title=Inferior: How Science Got Women Wrong – and the New Research That's Rewriting the Story|last=Saini|first=Angela|date=2017|publisher=Beacon Press|isbn=9780807071700|language=en}}</ref> She described the relationship between [[sociobiology]] and feminism as 'complex and multidimensional'.<ref>{{Citation|last=Tang-Martinez|first=Zuleyma|date=1997|pages=116–150|publisher=Springer US|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4615-5985-6_6|isbn=9780412073618|title=Feminism and Evolutionary Biology|chapter=The Curious Courtship of Sociobiology and Feminism: A Case of Irreconcilable Differences}}</ref>
Tang-Martinez and her students studied a broad range of topics and species, including the social systems of rodents (gerbils, voles, hamsters, black-tailed prairie dogs, eastern chipmunks, deer mice, and capybaras), as well as other mammals ( e.g., raccoons, otters).<ref name="Tang-Martínez 1212–1227">{{Cite journal|last=Tang-Martínez|first=Zuleyma|date=November 2003|journal=Journal of Mammalogy|language=en|volume=84|issue=4|pages=1212–1227|doi=10.1644/BLe-015|issn=0022-2372|title=Emerging Themes and Future Challenges: Forgotten Rodents, Neglected Questions|doi-access=free}}</ref>  Examples of her research include  using habituation-discrimination to study the ability of voles and other mammals to detect individually-distinct odors.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tang-Martínez|first1=Zuleyma|last2=Bixler|first2=Andrea|date=April 2009|title=Individual Discrimination by Odors in Sibling Prairie Voles (Microtus ochrogaster)|journal=Journal of Chemical Ecology|language=en|volume=35|issue=4|pages=400–404|doi=10.1007/s10886-009-9622-8|pmid=19373513|bibcode=2009JCEco..35..400T |s2cid=23571843|issn=0098-0331}}</ref>

Tang-Martinez became  associate professor in 1982 and full professor in 1994.<ref name=":1" /> She was director of women's studies between 1989 and 1990, and interim chair of her biology department in 1990.<ref name=":1" /> She has been concerned about students as higher education becomes more corporate.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://louisville.edu/journal/workplace/tang-martinez.html|title=Workplace Features: Zuleyma Tang-Martinez|last=bcaspar|website=louisville.edu|access-date=November 12, 2018|archive-date=December 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191216013216/http://louisville.edu/journal/workplace/tang-martinez.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1993 she became  president of the Animal Behavior Society.<ref name=":2" /> During her term in the presidential sequence of ABS (a 4-year commitment), she created the ethnic diversity fund, which supports scientists from underrepresented groups to attend academic conferences.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://urban-science.blogspot.com/2010/10/wise-latina-scientist.html|title=A Wise Latina Scientist|last=Dnlee|date=October 11, 2010|website=Urban Science Adventures! ©|access-date=November 12, 2018}}</ref> She also founded the Latin American Affairs Committee and served as its first chair.<ref name=":1" /> Currently (2020) she is the Animal Behavior Society  historian  and serves as an ex-officio member on the executive committee of the society.  In her duties as historian, she organized the first-ever symposium on the history of animal behavior, which was subsequently published as a special issue in the society journal, Animal Behaviour (vol. 164).<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.animalbehaviorsociety.org/web/about-officers.php|title=Animal Behavior Society|access-date=November 12, 2018|language=en}}</ref>

She retired in September 2011 and was made Founders Professor of Biology.<ref name=":0" /> In 2014 she edited (jointly with Ken Yasukawa) the first volume of the series  ''Animal Behavior: How and Why Animals Do The Things They Do''.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/10404561|title=Animal behavior : how and why animals do the things they do in SearchWorks catalog|website=searchworks.stanford.edu|language=en|access-date=November 12, 2018|isbn=9780313398704}}</ref> She remains part of a [[National Science Foundation]] proposal to develop the next generation of animal behavioural scientists (as Co-PI of "Weaving the Future of Animal Behavior").<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1833455&HistoricalAwards=false|title=NSF Award Search: Award#1833455 - Meeting: Weaving the Future of Animal Behavior; (2018–2021); Phoenix, AZ|website=nsf.gov|access-date=November 12, 2018}}</ref>

=== Awards and honours ===
* 1995 Scientists of Color, [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California at Berkeley]] ''[[O'Neil Ray Collins]] Distinguished Minority Scientist<ref name=":1" />''
* 1995 St. Louis Educational Equity Coalition ''Educational Equity Award for Higher Education<ref name=":1" />''
* 2002 Alzheimer's Association of St. Louis, ''Volunteer of the Year Award for contributions to public policy''
* 2006 Animal Behavior Society ''Exceptional Service Career Award''<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.animalbehaviorsociety.org/web/awards-service.php|title=Animal Behavior Society|access-date=November 12, 2018|language=en}}</ref>
* 2009 Animal Behavior Society ''Quest Award''<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.animalbehaviorsociety.org/web/awards-quest.php|title=Animal Behavior Society|access-date=November 12, 2018|language=en}}</ref>
* 2011 Animal Behavior Society, ''elected a Fellow''
* 2011 Hispanic Business magazine, selected as one of the top 100 most influential Hispanics in the US and one of the top 8 most influential academics
* 2022 Animal Behavior Society, Exemplar Award
* 2022 Inaugural speaker for Animal Behavior Society JEDI Plenary Lecture Series.

== Personal life ==
Tang-Martínez married her long-term partner, Arlene Zarembka, in Canada in 2005.<ref name="Springfield News-Leader">{{Cite news|url=https://eu.news-leader.com/story/news/local/ozarks/2014/08/17/sex-couple-speak-lawsuit-fight-equality/14215643/|title=Same-sex couple speak on lawsuit, fight for equality|work=Springfield News-Leader|access-date=November 12, 2018|language=en}}</ref> In 2014, she and Arlene campaigned for marriage equality as a plaintiffs in a successful lawsuit demanding that the state of Missouri recognize their Canadian marriage.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.stlmag.com/news/first-comes-love/|title=First Comes Love|last=Powell|first=William|date=July 24, 2014|access-date=November 12, 2018|language=en-US}}</ref> She is an advocate for Hispanics, other under-represented groups, and women in the sciences.<ref name="Springfield News-Leader"/><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://undark.org/article/mentorship-programs-science-technology/|title=For Minorities in Science, Building Communities Matters|work=Undark|access-date=November 12, 2018|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tang-Martinez|first=Zuleyma|date=August 1992|title=Women in Science: Demanding a Bigger Piece of the Pie or a New Recipe?|journal=Bulletin of Science, Technology & Society|language=en|volume=12|issue=4–5|pages=192–194|doi=10.1177/027046769201200402|s2cid=142428293|issn=0270-4676}}</ref>  She also is very civically involved: she serves as a commissioner on the St. Louis County Older Adults Commission, is a volunteer with the Alzheimer's Association of Greater St. Louis, serves on the research ethics committee of the Knight [[Alzheimer's disease|Alzheimer's Disease]] Research Center at the Washington University  in St Louis Medical school (for the "Adult Children" research project of the ADRC), is a member of a dialogue group, Shalom Amigos (American Jews, Latin American Jews, and non-Jewish Latinos), and serves on the board of directors of the UMSL Retiree Association.  She also has been a co-founder of two political groups in St. Louis (Privacy Rights Education Project or PREP founded in 1986 – now called PROMO and currently the primary state-wide LGBT advocacy group in Missouri) and MOmentum: Missouri Moving Forward, founded directly in response to the 2016 election.
